title: Life Saving Rules
body: When an LSR breach gets waved through as a routine "finding" instead of flagged for what it is, the corrective-action loop never closes. That's the exact gap the BUL fatality review turned up at ADW: four of the eight post-fatality controls — honking protocol, travel plan, six-day roster cap, site-discipline rules — still aren't confirmed as standing practice here.
keyPoints: Nine LSRs exist corporate-wide; four are live on your crew every shift — Mobile Equipment, Line of Fire, Geotechnical Ground Control, and Energy Isolation.
Enforcement isn't outcome-based. Per MSHEM-06.01 §5.1.11, action gets taken every time a rule is violated, whether or not anything actually went wrong that time.

Anyone on site — operator, contractor, visitor — has the right to stop unsafe work on the spot, without exposing themselves to risk and without fear of retaliation. That's an expectation for your foremen, not a courtesy.
A violation goes to the area supervisor first, who notifies HSS immediately; only an independent LSR Committee (HSS, Legal, HR) rules on whether it was intentional.

The six-consecutive-day roster limit from the BUL list isn't verified as an ADW control — and it lines up directly with the fatigue root cause already found in the DT-128 high-wall strike. Don't assume someone else is tracking it.
apply: Line-of-fire discipline at the loading face and on the ramps is the category that erodes fastest — it's the one most likely to get normalized into "that's just how we work the face," right up until it isn't.
